final_concept.name: Clearlane
final_concept.one_liner: A day planner for Torus-style stations on Utah's grid. It fills up in the midday clear lane, stays off the road in the 6pm jam and keeps Spin ready for Rocky Mountain Power's calls, all inside an hourly operating envelope RMP can audit.
final_concept.options_covered:
Option 1 (Rush hour for electrons) is the core. The race, the crash, the envelope and the backtest are all about when a station charges and discharges against PACE's day-ahead traffic.

Option 2 (Compute follows the sun) is covered by pointing the same engine at a flexible load. A SIMULATED 100 MW AI campus moves 25 MW for 3 hours from 6pm-9pm to 1pm-4pm, which is worth $2,551 at Oct 27 prices; the shape comes from Emerald AI's 256-GPU Phoenix test, which cut 25% for 3 hours. The where-vs-when card adds that in October, moving a 4-hour evening block in time saved 40-41%, while moving it across EDAM PacifiCorp/PGE nodes saved 8%. PACE was the cheapest of those nodes in 81% of hours (scratch-opt2).

The Option 2 insight: in Utah, compute should follow the sun in time, not in space.
final_concept.the_insight:
Utah's electric rush hour is 6pm, and the clear lane is midday, not overnight. The old off-peak habit runs backwards.

(1) Oct 27 PACE day-ahead LMP (CAISO OASIS, ELAP_PACE-APND, research/data/pace_snapshot_2026-10-27.csv):
- The five overnight hours from 1am to 6am average $38.71/MWh. The eight hours from 9am to 5pm average $22.83.
- The 3pm hour is $21.38 and the 6pm hour is $55.78, a 2.6x jump.
- Solar falls from 2,056 MW at 4pm to 36 MW at 6pm. Net load climbs 3,654.5 MW, from 604.6 MW in the 3pm hour to 4,259.1 MW in the 6pm hour.

(2) It is not one day. In October the day's largest upward price step landed in the 5pm or 6pm hour on 24 of 27 days, with a median step of $15.1 (scratch-opt2/step_hours_output.txt). July is messier: steps spread from 1pm to 8pm, median $10.1. That is why the plan backtests May 1 to Oct 27.

(3) Cheap and clean line up. In October the priciest 10% of hours averaged $67.3/MWh and 85.1% fossil; the cheapest 10% averaged $23.0 and 39.8% (join_analysis_output.txt). EIA average CO2 for PACE runs about 698 g/kWh overnight, 468 at midday and 665 in the evening.

(4) So, at Oct 27 prices, for a 1 MW / 2 MWh battery (RTE 0.88 is an ASSUMPTION; habit.py):
- Fixed overnight schedule (charge 1am-5am, discharge 6pm-8pm): $20.06 per MW-day.
- Clearlane timetable (charge 1pm-4pm, discharge 6pm-8pm): $58.41 per MW-day, 2.9x.
- At the 70 MW MOU scale: $1,405 vs $4,088 a day. This is value to RMP's system at day-ahead prices, not Torus revenue.
- CO2 at 70 MW: the overnight schedule adds about 18.4 t a day; the timetable avoids about 18.9 t. These are average-emissions estimates, not marginal.

(5) The less obvious half: daily scheduling and RMP's surprise calls compete for power, not energy.
- A 5.5-minute call at 0.5C uses about 4.6% of a Pulse. The 359 calls in 2025 add up to about 33 hours, 0.38% of the year.
- Spin sized to the enrolled kW holds 0.1 kWh per kW, enough for one 6-minute call, and recharges in about 6 minutes (half its published 12-minute discharge-and-recharge cycle). So Pulse can run the timetable at full power and needs spare power only during Spin's refill window.
- Holding the reserve in the battery instead costs about 3.4% of value, under an ASSUMED call of 25% of power (scratch-demo-story/fix.py), or it misses calls. A price-only plan could not have answered between 14% and 77% of 2025-pattern calls; which end applies depends only on whether Torus's 2025 heatmap is read as Mountain time or UTC.
final_concept.torus_tie:
**Spin.** Clearlane gives Spin the job its published specs fit (10C, full discharge in 6 minutes, discharge and recharge in 12 minutes, 25,000 cycles). It is the reserve for RMP's calls, sized to the enrolled kW at 0.1 kWh per kW, so Pulse never has to hold one.

**Pulse.** The timetable spends Pulse's published 7,500 cycles over 25 years at a calibrated wear price, keeping the plan near 300 cycles a year, with a meter on screen. A fixed nightly cycle would use 365. This puts Torus's own FAQ line into practice: Spin absorbs spikes so Pulse can discharge steadily.

**Lasso.** Torus publishes that Lasso already forecasts facility load, dispatches in under 250 ms, routes between Spin and Pulse, keeps an event audit log, schedules from facility load, rate schedules and grid signals, and lets smaller utilities and co-ops schedule against forecasts. Clearlane replaces none of that. Two things are not advertised:
- a timetable keyed to EDAM day-ahead prices at ELAP_PACE-APND, posted by about 9:16pm MT for the next day;
- an exportable hourly operating envelope with System Critical Hours.
Both are inputs Lasso could take through its API as one more grid signal.

**Wattsmart and RMP.** Torus is one of two approved commercial vendors in Wattsmart Battery (30 kW to 1.2 MW, IEEE 2030.5 with 30-second telemetry). Its 2025 record: 359 events, a 19 s ramp against a 30 s target, and 102% delivered against a 90-100% band. In its June 2026 ROWE comments, Torus asked regulators to credit 'controlled and scheduled dispatch', to set standards for 'aggregated and utility-directed operating envelopes' and to define 'System Critical Hours' transparently. Clearlane is a working example of that artifact with a three-policy backtest behind it, which is evidence Torus can take to the docket.

**Who captures the value.** The $4,088 a day at 70 MW is value to RMP's system at day-ahead prices, not Torus revenue. Today RMP dispatches and settles in EDAM, so RMP's customers capture it. Torus and hosts get a share only if a program credits scheduled dispatch, which is the ROWE ask. The MOU is 70 MW, now up to 500 MW; that is a ceiling, not installed capacity. Wyoming's DSM plan already allows 'daily load cycling'; the Utah plan does not say so.

**Hosts.** Demand charges are about half of a C&I bill and are set by a single 15- or 30-minute interval (Torus-published). Clearlane's host lane caps Pulse charging and Spin refills under the host's 15-minute ceiling, so the grid timetable never sets a new host peak. That protects what Torus sells hosts: pricing from $549 a month, and Creekstone Delta's 'Torus Load Smoothing'.

**Data centers.** Torus's data-center pages returned 404 from Aug 4 to Oct 26 2026, so Clearlane makes no claim about a Torus data-center product. The Option 2 card shows the same timetable applied to flexible compute as a SIMULATED case.
final_concept.demo_script:
**Setup.** Demo laptop, browser full screen at 1920x1080, DATA_MODE=snapshot. Bundle is Oct 28 (today), with Oct 27 as the fallback; the date is always on screen. Words in braces are read from public/derived/numbers.json. Oct 27 values are in brackets for rehearsal. Total 2:45.

**Beat 1, 0:00-0:25, Traffic report.** Screen: the ribbon (24 hours as a road colored clear, shoulder and jam), with solar falling and net load climbing.
Say: 'This is today's traffic report for Utah's grid, published last night by the western day-ahead market. The road is clear at midday while solar runs. Then net load climbs {net_load_climb_mw} [3,654] megawatts in three hours, and the price jumps {peak_over_trough} [2.6] times by 6pm. In October that jump landed at 5 or 6pm on 24 of 27 days. Torus's CTO describes the grid as a freeway at 5pm on a Friday. Clearlane is the traffic app.'

**Beat 2, 0:25-0:55, The race (Space).** Screen: on the left, 'Battery on the off-peak rule'; on the right, 'Simulated Torus-style station on Clearlane'. A 15-second time-lapse of the day plays with Spin and Pulse bars, the host's 15-minute meter under its ceiling line, and a cycles meter. End cards show $/MW-day and $/day at 70 MW, with the caveat line 'Average-emissions estimate (EIA hourly); marginal emissions can differ.'
Say: 'Same battery, same evening. The off-peak rule charges overnight at {overnight_avg} [$39], in Utah's dirtiest hours. Clearlane charges at {midday_avg} [$22], in the cleanest. That is {fixed_usd_mw_day} [$20] against {clearlane_usd_mw_day} [$58] a megawatt-day, and the host's meter never crosses its ceiling. At Torus's 70 megawatts that is {fixed_70} [$1,405] against {clearlane_70} [$4,088] a day of value to RMP's system, and about {co2_avoided_70} [19] tonnes of CO2 a day avoided instead of {co2_added_70} [18] added.'

**Beat 3, 0:55-1:40, The crash (C, at about 6:40pm in the time-lapse).** Screen: the banner 'Rocky Mountain Power call: {enrolled_kw} kW now'. The time-lapse pauses and an inset plays the 6-minute call in about 5 seconds. It shows requested vs Spin vs Pulse kW, and Spin draining, then refilling under the host ceiling. A ghost battery-only station beside it runs the same call. The event card shows Torus-published 2025 facts (359 events; 19 s ramp vs a 30 s target; 102% delivered vs a 90-100% band) apart from our SIMULATED result. Then press C again inside the refill window.
Say: 'Now RMP calls, unannounced, the way it did 359 times last year. Everyone assumes the battery is busy. But a six-minute call needs power, not energy: about 5 percent of a Pulse. Spin, sized to the enrolled kilowatts, answers on its own while Pulse stays in its lane. Then Spin refills in six minutes without setting a new demand peak for the host. A battery-only plan has to hold power back all evening, which costs it about 3.4 percent of its value, or it misses the call. Press it again during the refill: the call still wins, Pulse gives up part of its block, and the card shows exactly what was short.'

**Beat 4, 1:40-2:00, Re-plan.** Screen: the plan redraws from the batteries' actual state, labeled 'Re-planned in {solve_ms} ms' (measured live with performance.now()). The cycles meter reads {cycles_today} against a budget of 0.82 a day.
Say: 'Clearlane re-plans the rest of the day from where both batteries actually are, in {solve_ms} milliseconds on this laptop. It stays inside Pulse's cycle budget: 7,500 cycles over 25 years is 300 a year, not one every night.'

**Beat 5, 2:00-2:25, Envelope and proof (E, then B).** Screen: the 24-hour envelope, with System Critical Hours shaded, reserve kW, max charge and discharge kW, and a Copy JSON button. Then the backtest card: May 1 to Oct 27, three policies, P10-P90 bars of $/MW-day, cycles per year, and calls missed under each heatmap reading.
Say: 'Every evening Clearlane exports this: an hourly operating envelope with System Critical Hours, the artifact Torus asked Utah regulators to standardize in June. And it is not one good day. From May 1 to October 27 it beat the off-peak rule on {share_days_beating}% of days, at {clearlane_p10} to {clearlane_p90} a megawatt-day, and Spin answered {calls_answered_pct}% of simulated calls.'

**Beat 6, 2:25-2:45, Scale and close (slider, then close card).** Screen: a fleet slider from 70 MW to the 500 MW ceiling, with the caveat 'Assumes the fleet does not move prices', then the Option 2 line and the close card.
Say: 'Same engine, any flexible load. An AI campus that moves a quarter of its load for three hours into the clear lane saves {campus_usd} [$2,551] a day at these prices. In Utah, compute should follow the sun in time, not in space. Clearlane: fill up when the road is clear, and keep Spin ready for the crash.'

The live RTM tile sits in a corner showing 'Snapshot, <time>' unless a fetch succeeded in the last 15 minutes. It is never narrated and never the close. If rehearsal 3 runs over time, drop the second press first and keep the one sentence about it.
final_concept.wow_moment:
Halfway through the time-lapse, at the 6pm peak, an RMP call drops onto a station that is already discharging. The day freezes and a 6-minute inset plays in 5 seconds:
- Spin answers alone at the enrolled kW while Pulse holds its block.
- Spin refills under the host's 15-minute ceiling.
- The battery-only ghost beside it misses the call.
- Clearlane re-plans the rest of the day, and the measured milliseconds appear on screen.
Then a second press during the refill proves the rule: the call still wins, Pulse diverts power, and the shortfall is shown, not hidden.
final_concept.architecture:
A static, offline-first web app built around a pure engine.

(1) prep/ (Python 3.13 stdlib only, run with python -I) fetches CAISO OASIS (PRC_LMP DAM, SLD_FCST DAM, EDAM_WND_SLR_FORECAST_GRP) and EIA (930 six-month CSVs, the 930-api, PACE.xlsx hourly CO2). It joins every source on UTC interval start and writes:
- public/data/bundle_<day>.json (one Mountain calendar day);
- hist_2026-05-01_2026-10-27.json;
- torus_published.json.
These are precomputed and committed.

(2) engine/ (pure TypeScript, no DOM, no network) holds lanes, the 15-minute DP, the three policies, the crash simulation, re-plan, envelope, backtest and the Option 2 shift. The same code runs in the browser on stage (solve, crash, re-plan, each timed with performance.now()) and from node CLIs (engine/cli/backtest.ts and numbers.ts via tsx). The CLIs write public/derived/backtest.json, numbers.json and envelope_<day>.json.

(3) app/ (Vite + React 18, hand-written SVG charts, system fonts, no CDN) reads bundle and derived JSON and calls the engine for every plan and crash shown. It is keyboard-driven through the six beats.

(4) Optional: api/rtm.ts, a Vercel function that proxies the latest OASIS 5-minute PACE price, because OASIS has no CORS. The app shows it only when it is fresh.

Data flow: OASIS/EIA -> prep -> public/data (REAL) -> engine CLIs -> public/derived (DERIVED) -> app and pitch. Pitch and UI read every number from numbers.json, so a Tue-night regeneration updates the stage and the deck together.

- Precomputed: bundles, history, backtest, numbers.json.
- Live on stage: the day's DP solve, the crash, the re-plan and its timing, envelope export, the time-zone toggle.
- DATA_MODE=snapshot is the default, and nothing on stage needs the network.
final_concept.data_plan:
Classes: REAL = public data as published; DERIVED = our code on REAL inputs; SIMULATED = synthetic; TORUS-PUBLISHED = Torus's own published numbers; ASSUMPTION = a value we chose, always shown with a chip.

**Sources:**
1. CAISO OASIS PRC_LMP DAM (version=12, resultformat=6) for ELAP_PACE-APND, plus ELAP_PACW-APND, ELAP_PGE-APND and TH_SP15_GEN (use the exact node ids from the research scripts). REAL. Covers the Oct 27 and Oct 28 bundles and May 1 to Oct 27 history. Oct 28 prices post by about 9:16pm MT on Oct 27.
2. CAISO SLD_FCST DAM for PACE. REAL. Operating day only.
3. CAISO EDAM_WND_SLR_FORECAST_GRP GroupZip (XML) for PACE solar and wind. REAL, with negative night solar clamped to 0. Published about 9:10am PT the day before.
4. Net load = load minus solar minus wind. DERIVED.
5. EIA PACE.xlsx hourly generated-basis CO2 (lb/kWh x 453.592 = g/kWh). REAL observed average for history. For the operating day, a trailing 30-day hour-of-day mean, DERIVED, because EIA lags about a day.
6. EIA-930 six-month balance CSVs and the 930-api for PACE demand, forecast and fuel mix. REAL. Used for headroom and fuel-share cards; flag the bad 1,137 MW hour on Jan 8.
7. CAISO PRC_INTVL_LMP RTM 5-minute price. REAL. Optional live tile only, through api/rtm.ts.
8. Torus numbers (Spin and Pulse specs, 2025 Wattsmart stats, by-hour and by-weekday counts, MOU sizes). TORUS-PUBLISHED, stored in torus_published.json with a URL per value.
9. Host load and host ceiling. SIMULATED weekday C&I shape that peaks mid-afternoon, so the host ceiling actually binds on midday charging.
10. RMP call times. SIMULATED, sampled from the 2025 counts with a fixed seed.
11. RTE 0.88, the 25%-of-power call for the battery-only contrast, the export limit, and demand charge $/kW-month: ASSUMPTION. The tariff stays unverified until the Tue check. The OpenEI transcription shows $13.27 and $11.74 with season labels lost. A 2020 ChargePoint filing describes Schedule 6A on-peak as 7am-11pm weekdays, and an Oct 2025 RMP filing proposes new 6A periods from AMI data; both come from search summaries only. Host results show in kW until the tariff is verified.
12. Lanes, System Critical Hours, wear price, envelope, backtest and the Option 2 shift: DERIVED.
13. Headroom card (1,265 MW at 0.5% curtailment) and where-vs-when card (40-41% vs 8%; 81%): DERIVED, from research scratch-depth and scratch-opt2.
14. Open-Meteo: not used. Its license is CC BY 4.0 non-commercial, and Salt Lake City irradiance is a poor proxy for PACE solar.

**Fetch rules:** under 31 days per OASIS call (31 returns error 1004); at least 5 s between calls, with 30 s backoff on HTTP 429; GMT timestamps with Pacific OPR_HR. A Mountain day is the 24 hours from 06:00Z (MDT, UTC-6, until Nov 1). Hour 0 comes from the previous CAISO operating day and is noted in the bundle.

**Cached-snapshot fallback:** every bundle, the history, torus_published.json and all derived JSON are committed. Snapshot mode loads only local files. If the Tue 9:15pm refresh fails by 10pm, the stage stays on the Oct 27 bundle and says so. The live tile shows 'Snapshot, <timestamp>' whenever its last fetch is older than 15 minutes or failed.
final_concept.core_algorithms:
1) **Lanes** (DERIVED, pinned). Per Mountain day:
- clear = hours priced at or below the day's minimum plus 25% of its range;
- jam = hours at or above the maximum minus 25%;
- shoulder = everything else.
On Oct 27 that gives clear 9am-5pm ($21.38-28.61), shoulder 5pm-6pm ($34.03), and jam 6pm-midnight ($52.42-55.78, with a 6pm-11pm core of $54.10-55.78). Labels and dollar ranges are always computed, never typed. System Critical Hours (our proposal, labeled as ours) = the day's 4 highest net-load hours plus every jam hour.

2) **Planner.** A deterministic dynamic program over Pulse state of charge:
- 96 fifteen-minute steps, with each hourly day-ahead price held for 4 steps;
- 41 SoC levels; an action moves to the next level within Pulse power, and 0.5C allows at most 5 levels per step;
- charge and discharge efficiency are each sqrt(RTE), with RTE 0.88 (ASSUMPTION).
Objective: maximize sum(price x grid MWh) minus the wear price W x discharged MWh.
Hard constraints:
- host meter (host load + Pulse + Spin) at or below the host's 15-minute ceiling every step;
- export at or below export_limit_kw;
- in System Critical Hours, Pulse discharge at or below pulse_kw minus max(0, enrolled_kw minus Spin available kW), so with Spin full, Pulse runs at full power;
- terminal SoC at least the starting SoC.
About 43k transition evaluations per solve, so the solve and re-plan run in the browser and are timed on stage.

3) **Wear price** (DERIVED). Pulse's published 7,500 cycles over 25 years is a budget of 300 cycles a year. Bisect W in [0, 60] $/MWh so the Clearlane policy uses at most 300 full-equivalent cycles a year across the backtest. Start at W = 10, which held about one cycle a day in fix.py. The cycles meter shows today against 0.82 a day.

4) **Policies.**
- Fixed overnight schedule: charge 1am-5am, discharge 6pm-8pm. This is the off-peak rule and is never presented as Torus practice.
- Price-only: the DP with W = 0, no envelope, no host ceiling and no Spin reserve. This is the battery-only strawman.
- Clearlane: the DP with calibrated W, the envelope, the host ceiling and Spin reserved.

5) **Crash.** A 1-second simulation of a SIMULATED call at enrolled kW for 330 s, with the TORUS-PUBLISHED 19 s ramp.
- Spin serves first; sized to enrolled kW at 0.1 kWh per kW, it covers a 6-minute call.
- Pulse covers any remainder from its spare power.
- Spin then recharges at min(spin_kw, host ceiling minus host load minus planned Pulse charge): 6 minutes if uncapped, inside the published 12-minute discharge and recharge.
- Second-press rule: a call during the refill always wins; Pulse diverts from its block, and shortfall_kwh is reported.
- The DP then re-plans from the actual SoC. The battery-only ghost replays the same call against the price-only plan.

6) **Event sampler.** Poisson with a mean of 359/365 calls a day. Hours come from Torus's 2025 by-hour counts [9,41,5,4,1,3,4,14,23,26,25,20,15,33,19,14,14,8,6,4,5,34,24,8] and weekday weights from [50,57,43,57,53,45,54], with a fixed seed. Every result is run twice, reading the heatmap as Mountain time and as UTC (shift 6 h), because the source states no time zone.

7) **Backtest.** Every Mountain day from May 1 to Oct 27 2026 (about 180 days, all MDT), all three policies, on REAL day-ahead prices and REAL EIA hourly CO2. Reports:
- P10, P50, P90 and mean of $/MW-day and t CO2/MW-day;
- cycles per year;
- calls unanswerable under each heatmap reading;
- host-ceiling breaches;
- share of days on which Clearlane beats the off-peak rule.
Missing days are listed, never filled.

8) **Envelope.** Per hour: fleet reserve kW, max charge kW after host ceilings, max discharge kW, planned kW, the System Critical flag and a plain-words reason. Schema clearlane.envelope/v1. Fields are chosen to map onto IEEE 2030.5 DER control limits; verify the 2030.5 field names before claiming that on stage.

9) **Option 2 shift.** Move a flexible block (MW x hours) from the day's priciest hours to the cheapest hours inside an allowed window. Oct 27: a SIMULATED 100 MW campus moves 25 MW for 3 h from 6pm-9pm to 1pm-4pm, which is 75 MWh and $2,551 (pinned).

10) **Pinned tests.** The TypeScript engine reproduces prep/reference/habit.py and fix.py to the cent on the Oct 27 fixture. DP outputs are then snapshot-pinned, and one deliberate mutation per safety constraint (host ceiling, reserve, terminal SoC) proves the tests can fail.

final_concept.nucleus_fit:
The Nucleus x Startup State $10K bounty is a possible double entry; ask the organizers Tue 8am whether it is allowed and whether it needs a separate submission. Mapping to its rubric:
- **Progress (30%):** a working engine with pinned tests, a live re-plan on real CAISO and EIA data, and a 180-day backtest. Show the train tags and test count.
- **Path to reality (25%):** Torus already ran 359 Wattsmart events for RMP in 2025 and asked regulators for operating envelopes and System Critical Hours. Clearlane's envelope is that artifact. The next step is a pilot that feeds Lasso a day-ahead schedule at a few Wattsmart sites.
- **Hard tech depth (20%):** two-speed storage physics (10C Spin vs 0.5C Pulse); a 15-minute DP with host-meter, export and reserve constraints; cycle-budget wear pricing; EDAM market-data plumbing; an envelope mapped to 2030.5 control limits.
- **Utah impact (15%):** the PACE headroom card. About 1,265 MW of new flexible load fits under the last 12 months' PACE peak if it curtails 0.5% of hours: 184 hours, 124 of them in July, with 90% of those hours needing no more than 50% curtailment. This is DERIVED from EIA-930 (scratch-depth/headroom_output.txt). Add 70 MW today and the 500 MW ceiling.
- **Team and pitch (10%):** a solo founder running an agent team, with the lanes table and train log as evidence.
This lives on one added slide (slide 9). Angela Smith, Nucleus COO, also sits on the Torus panel, so the slide earns its place either way.
risks: OASIS is down or returns HTTP 429 at Tue 9:15pm. Mitigation: backoff, and a hard stop at 10pm. The Oct 27 bundle stays on stage, labeled with its date.

Oct 28 turns out to be a weak day (cloud, small spread). Mitigation: open on today honestly and anchor the insight on the backtest P50 and the 24-of-27 October pattern. Keep Oct 27 as the worked example.

Overclaiming about Torus. Mitigation: say 'not advertised', never 'Torus lacks'. Stations are 'simulated Torus-style'. The off-peak rule is never shown as Torus practice. Grok reviews every train for this.
The heatmap time zone is unknown. Mitigation: always show both readings (a 14% to 77% price-only miss rate) and ask Torus Tue morning.
Average vs marginal CO2. Mitigation: a caveat line on every CO2 end card, and never lead with CO2. WattTime marginal data is free only for CAISO_NORTH.
The C&I tariff is unverified. Mitigation: host results show in kW. Tariff dollars and the 'tariff and market clocks disagree' framing appear only if Tuesday's check verifies them.
The price-taker assumption fails at scale. 500 MW is about 8% of the Oct 27 PACE load peak of 6,024 MW. Mitigation: a caveat on the scale slider.

The event baseline and export rules are unknown (does delivery count against scheduled output or the meter? are sites allowed to export?). Mitigation: export_limit_kw is an ASSUMPTION parameter, and both questions go to Torus.
An engine bug on stage. Mitigation: pinned tests against the Python reference, a mutation check per constraint, freeze at 2pm, and the backup video.
Laptop, projector or Wi-Fi failure. Mitigation: offline build, USB copy, the Mac as a second machine, and the 2:45 backup video.
Solo fatigue. Mitigation: protected sleep blocks and hard cut checkpoints at Tue 1pm and 5pm.
Contract churn between lanes. Mitigation: freeze at Train 1; changes go only through Integration.
The scratchpad research could be cleared. Mitigation: copy it into research/ in the first 40 minutes.
Double-entry or public-repo rules are unknown. Mitigation: ask organizers Tue 8am, and keep keys out of the repo so it can go public at any time.
questions_for_torus: In Lasso today, what sets a Station's daily charging window at an RMP Wattsmart site: the host's rate schedule, an RMP signal, or both?
After a Wattsmart event, does Spin refill from Pulse or from the grid, and is that refill capped by the host's demand?
What time zone is the 2025 event heatmap on the Rocky Mountain Power case study in?
Who sets the reserve kW at each site: RMP, Lasso or the enrollment contract?
Is event delivery measured against the station's scheduled output or against the site meter's baseline?
Do Wattsmart sites export to the grid, or is discharge limited to the host's own load?
Does Lasso accept an external day-ahead schedule or operating envelope through its API?

pitch_outline:
On stage: slide 1, then the live demo, then slide 11. Slides 2 and 4-10 are Q&A backups. Every number is a {key} read from public/derived/numbers.json. No em dashes.

1. Title. "Clearlane. Fill up when Utah's grid is clear. Keep Spin ready for the crash." Line: Torus bounty, Option 1 with an Option 2 lens. Team line.
2. "Utah's rush hour is 6pm." The ribbon image and three numbers: overnight average {overnight_avg}, midday average {midday_avg}, 6pm price {peak_price}. Caption: "The biggest price jump landed at 5 or 6pm on 24 of 27 October days." Line: "In October the cheapest hours were also the cleanest: 39.8% fossil vs 85.1% in the priciest."
3. Live demo, six beats, 2:45: traffic report, race, crash, re-plan, envelope and proof, scale and close.
4. "Power, not energy." A six-minute call at 0.5C uses about 4.6% of a Pulse. All 359 calls in 2025 add up to about 33 hours a year. Spin holds 0.1 kWh per kW, enough for one call, and refills in six minutes under the host's ceiling. Torus's own line: Spin absorbs spikes so Pulse can discharge steadily.
5. "Not one good day." The backtest chart, May 1 to Oct 27, three policies: P10 to P90 of dollars per MW-day, cycles per year against the 300 budget, and calls answered under both heatmap readings.
6. "The envelope Torus asked for." An hourly envelope JSON beside three short phrases from Torus's June 2026 ROWE comments: credit for controlled and scheduled dispatch, standards for operating envelopes, and transparently defined System Critical Hours.
7. "Where it plugs in." Lasso forecasts, dispatches in under 250 ms and routes Spin and Pulse. Clearlane adds what is not advertised: a day-ahead market timetable and an exportable envelope, as one more grid signal. Line: "Value to RMP's system at day-ahead prices, not Torus revenue. RMP's customers capture it today; Torus and hosts share it if scheduled dispatch is credited."
8. "Compute follows the sun, in time." Moving a 4-hour evening block in time saved 40 to 41 percent; moving it across EDAM nodes saved 8 percent. PACE was the cheapest node in 81 percent of October hours. A SIMULATED AI campus shift: {campus_usd} a day.
9. "Utah impact" (the Nucleus slide). PACE could absorb about 1,265 MW of new flexible load at 0.5 percent curtailment (184 hours, mostly July). 70 MW today, 500 MW ceiling. Path to reality: a Lasso pilot at a few Wattsmart sites.
10. "What is real." A compact provenance table (REAL, DERIVED, SIMULATED, TORUS-PUBLISHED, ASSUMPTION), the assumptions, and the questions we asked Torus.
11. Close. "Clearlane: fill up when the road is clear, keep Spin ready for the crash." Ask: "Let us feed Lasso a day-ahead envelope at three Wattsmart sites this winter."
anticipated_judge_questions: Isn't this what Lasso already does? Lasso forecasts load, dispatches in under 250 ms, routes Spin and Pulse, and already schedules against forecasts for co-ops (Torus-published). Clearlane adds two things Torus does not advertise, a timetable keyed to EDAM day-ahead prices and an exportable envelope, and Lasso could take both through its API as one more grid signal.

Who actually gets the $4,088 a day? Nobody, as revenue: it is value to RMP's system at day-ahead prices. RMP dispatches and settles in EDAM, so its customers capture it today; Torus and hosts share it only if a program credits scheduled dispatch, which is the ask in Torus's June 2026 ROWE comments.

Is October 27 cherry-picked? The backtest card covers every day from May 1 to Oct 27 and shows the P10-P90 range. October is the clean case (24 of 27 days put the biggest jump at 5 or 6pm); July is messier (median step $10.1, spread from 1pm to 8pm), and we show that too.
Why not just charge overnight like everyone does? On Oct 27 the overnight hours averaged $38.71 against $22.83 at midday. EIA's average CO2 for PACE is about 698 g/kWh overnight and 468 at midday.

What happens when RMP calls during the jam, when the battery is busy? The call needs power, not energy, and Spin sized to the enrolled kW covers a 6-minute call alone. If a second call lands during Spin's 6-minute refill, Pulse diverts power and the card shows any shortfall.

Doesn't midday charging blow up the host's demand charge? The planner treats the host's 15-minute ceiling as a hard constraint for both Pulse charging and Spin refills, and the meter line on screen never crosses it. We show the result in kW because the tariff dollars are not verified yet.
Average or marginal emissions? Average: EIA hourly generated-basis CO2 for PACE, and the end card says so. Marginal data (WattTime) is free only for CAISO_NORTH, so we do not lead with CO2.

What does this do to Pulse's cycle life? Torus publishes 7,500 cycles over 25 years, a budget of 300 a year. The wear price is calibrated to that budget and a meter shows it; a fixed nightly cycle would use 365 a year.

How do you know when the calls happen? Torus's 2025 heatmap gives counts by hour and weekday but states no time zone. We run both readings, and a price-only plan's miss rate swings from 14% to 77% between them, which is why the reserve has to sit in Spin.

Is Utah even allowed to cycle these daily? Wyoming's DSM plan explicitly allows daily load cycling; Utah's plan does not say so. That is part of what the envelope and the ROWE ask are meant to settle.

What is real and what is simulated? Prices, forecasts and CO2 come from CAISO and EIA. Torus specs and 2025 stats are Torus-published. The stations, host load and call times are simulated, and every number on screen carries a chip saying which.

Does 500 MW move the price? Probably: 500 MW is about 8% of PACE's Oct 27 peak load of 6,024 MW, so the price-taker assumption breaks at scale. The slider says so, and 500 MW is the MOU ceiling, not installed capacity.

Why a DP and not machine learning? Day-ahead prices are known the evening before, so the price leg needs no forecast. An exact DP over 96 steps solves in milliseconds and is auditable, while forecasting load stays Lasso's job.

What about data centers (Option 2)? The same engine moves a flexible block in time: a simulated 25 MW for 3 hours is worth $2,551 on Oct 27. In October, time-shifting beat place-shifting 40% to 8%, and PACE was the cheapest EDAM node in 81% of hours.

Do Utah's tariffs agree with the market? Possibly not. A 2020 filing described Schedule 6A on-peak as 7am to 11pm weekdays, and a 2025 filing proposes new periods, but we have not verified current hours. That is a policy finding to check, not a claim.

What would you need from Torus to make this real? Four things: how Spin refills, how event delivery is baselined, whether sites export, and an API route for an external schedule or envelope. Then a pilot at a few Wattsmart sites.
stack_decision:
- **Data prep: Python 3.13, standard library only.** urllib, zipfile, csv, json and xml.etree, always run as `python -I`. This keeps the prep lane dependency-free and reproducible on any machine. It also matches the research scripts, which become reference implementations and test oracles.
- **Engine: pure TypeScript.** No DOM and no network, so the exact code that pinned tests check is the code that runs live on stage in the browser. The node CLIs (backtest, numbers) run it through tsx.
- **App: Vite plus React 18 (react@18.3.1).** Charts are hand-written SVG, fonts are a system stack, and nothing loads from a CDN, so the build runs from `vite preview` or a static folder with Wi-Fi off.
- **Tests:** vitest for the engine and app, unittest for prep, and one `npm run check` gate (typecheck, test, build).
- **Hosting:** none required. The stage build is local. An optional Vercel function (api/rtm.ts) proxies OASIS for the live tile only, because OASIS sends no CORS headers.
- **Versions:** pinned at install time through the lockfile.
- **Rejected:** a Python web backend (one more process to fail on stage), a chart library (projector tuning is easier in raw SVG), and any live dependency in the demo path.
